title: Partitioning
summary:
Partitioning is the **logical** half of sharding: data is grouped into partitions, and a separate mapping decides which nodes hold each partition. (Convention used here: *partition* = logical unit of data and routing, *shard* = where it lives. Many systems use the words interchangeably.)

The usual chain:

1. The client supplies a **partition key** and so decides which logical partition a row belongs to.
2. The partition key is hashed with [consistent hashing](#/sd/f/consistent-hashing) to a **token**.
3. A **keyring** assigns token ranges to nodes. The node that owns the token is the **primary replica**.
4. The other replicas are picked by a placement policy, for example across availability zones and racks.

So **one token range corresponds to one replica set**: `[100, 500] -> {A, B, C}`. Replication, rebalancing and failure handling all operate on token ranges, not on individual rows.

Why it matters: the partition key is the one decision that is hard to change later. A low-cardinality key (country) caps your parallelism; a skewed key creates hot partitions; and rows that must be read or written together should share a partition key so they stay in one replica set. Using many more partitions than nodes lets you rebalance by moving whole partitions (see [token rebalancing](#/sd/f/token-rebalancing) and [hash bucketing](#/sd/f/hash-bucketing)).

drills.q: A chat service sets `partitionKey = country`. It has 40 nodes and about 200 countries, but 35% of users are in one country. What is the main risk?
options: Low cardinality plus skew: one partition (one replica set) carries a third of the load and cannot be split by the key
Replicas cannot be placed across zones
Tokens will no longer be assigned to nodes
drills.explain: All rows with the same partition key land in one token position, so a dominant value cannot be spread by the hash. Pick a higher-cardinality key, or add a sub-key, so the hash has something to distribute.

drills.q: Order the path from a request to the node that serves it as primary.
items: The client supplies the partition key
The key is hashed to a token
The keyring finds the token range containing the token
The token range maps to a replica set
The first replica (the token owner) is the primary
drills.explain: The mapping is key -> token -> range -> replica set. Nothing about the row itself names a node, which is what lets the keyring move ranges without changing keys.

drills.q: A token range has replicas A, B, C, all in rack 4 of one zone. The rack's top-of-rack switch fails. What happens, and what should the placement policy have done?
options: The range becomes unavailable (and may lose data if the rack burns); replicas should be spread across racks and zones
Nothing: three replicas always survive any single failure
The range keeps serving because the keyring reassigns it instantly
Only the primary is affected because followers are independent of the rack
drills.explain: Replica count only protects against failures that are independent. Correlated failure domains (rack, zone) must be separated by placement. Otherwise three copies behave like one.

drills.q: Token space `[0, 1000)` is cut into 10 equal ranges. Replication factor 3, and ranges are placed so every node holds the same number of replicas. The cluster has 5 nodes. How many token ranges does each node store a replica of?
drills.explain: There are 10 ranges x 3 replicas = 30 replica placements, spread evenly over 5 nodes = 6 per node. Each node therefore holds 6/10 = 60% of the data.

drills.q: Why do many systems create far more logical partitions than nodes (for example 256 partitions on 8 nodes)?
options: So that rebalancing can move whole partitions instead of rehashing individual keys
So that every key gets its own replica set
Because a node can only serve one partition
drills.explain: Partitions are the unit of movement. With many small units a new node just takes a few of them; with one partition per node you would have to split data when scaling. A node can hold many partitions.

drills.q: Explain the difference between a partition and a node using the line `[100, 500] -> {A, B, C}`.
drills.answer: `[100, 500]` is a token range, a logical group of partitions; `{A, B, C}` is the replica set of nodes that physically store it, with the token owner as primary. Partitioning is the stable logical grouping; placement can change without changing which partition a key belongs to.
